title: Control Activities, Segregation of Duties & Multi-System Reconciliation (CMA P1-E · feeds AUD/ISC)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — one close crosses four systems

MBG environment: JCS is the job-cost GL; Ledgerline is used for MBG Multifamily and has a different chart of accounts; PayStream and Apex Staffing support payroll; First Regional Bank is the primary bank. Calling JCS “Ledgerline 100” collapses an important system boundary. Moving data among these systems creates risks in authorization, completeness, accuracy, cutoff, classification, and entity segregation.

No single reconciliation proves the close. The bank can show cash that never reached JCS. Payroll can be paid correctly but allocated to the wrong job. A Ledgerline account can be mapped incorrectly to the MBG chart. Control activities must be designed around the transaction flow, not around the assumption that one system is always right.

Concept — control activities and assertions

Control activities are actions established through policies and procedures to reduce risk. They can be preventive or detective, manual or automated, and entity-level or process-level. Common categories include approvals, verifications, reconciliations, physical controls, access controls, segregation of duties, and supervisory review.

Financial-reporting controls target assertions: occurrence/existence, completeness, accuracy/valuation, cutoff, classification, rights and obligations, and presentation. A control is well designed when a competent person could operate it and prevent or detect and correct the specified risk timely. Evidence that a policy exists is not evidence that the control operated.

Segregation of duties

Separate four incompatible functions when practical:

  • Authorization: approve vendors, purchases, payroll changes, JEs, and payments.
  • Custody: control cash, checks, credentials, or assets.
  • Recordkeeping: enter transactions and maintain ledgers.
  • Reconciliation/review: compare independent evidence and resolve differences.

A person who creates a vendor, changes its bank details, enters an invoice, and releases payment can perpetrate and conceal fraud. In a small team, compensating controls may include owner review of bank-positive-pay exceptions, independent vendor callbacks, audit-log review, and post-payment analytics. Compensation must address the same risk and operate with sufficient precision.

Worked process — payroll from source to WIP

Use the real system structure with illustrative amounts. Approved time supports $50,000 of gross job labor in PayStream, with $10,000 employee withholdings, $40,000 net ACH, and $6,000 employer taxes. The entry records $50,000 labor plus $6,000 employer burden, not $40,000 cash expense and not $66,000. Employee withholding is part of gross pay and becomes a liability.

Control pointRiskControl
Time approvalFictitious or wrong-job hoursSupervisor approves employee, job, hours, and period before payroll lock
Payroll calculationIncorrect rate or taxPayStream configuration and exception report reviewed independently
PaymentUnauthorized bank changeDual approval and independent change verification
JCS postingIncomplete or duplicate importControl totals, unique batch ID, and exact account/job mapping
ReconciliationPayroll, bank, and GL disagreeGross-to-net, liability, ACH, and WIP bridges resolved to $0.00

MBG's convention prohibits cash labor. All labor is PayStream ACH or MBG check. A control narrative must not normalize an illegal or unsupported cash workaround.

Multi-system reconciliation

For each interface, define source, destination, frequency, owner, control total, unique identifier, reject handling, and evidence. A good interface reconciliation proves:

  1. Completeness: every authorized source record reached the destination once.
  2. Accuracy: amounts, accounts, jobs, entities, dates, and descriptions mapped correctly.
  3. Cutoff: records landed in the intended period.
  4. Validity: destination records originated from approved source activity.

Assume an illustrative PayStream register contains 120 employee lines totaling $56,000 of gross labor and employer burden. JCS import contains 119 lines totaling $55,250. A total difference of $750 and count difference of one provide complementary evidence. Trace the missing unique employee/pay-period/job record; do not allocate $750 across jobs to force a tie.

When moving Ledgerline Multifamily data into group reporting, use a controlled crosswalk with source account, destination account, effective date, preparer, approver, and exception status. One-to-many or many-to-one mappings require explicit rules. MBG and Riverton bank accounts remain separate; cross-system integration never authorizes entity blending.

Checkbook and payment controls

Bank/checkbook configuration links the correct legal entity, GL cash account, bank account, payment method, approval workflow, and numbering sequence. MBG uses First Regional Bank account 102.1 “Main 850-149”; Riverton uses First Regional Bank account 102; Apex uses its own UCB account 104. A payment run from the wrong checkbook can be valid in amount yet wrong in entity and cash account.

Preventive controls restrict checkbook access and require approval. Detective controls compare payment files to bank activity, review sequence gaps, and reconcile bank to GL. Positive pay helps the bank identify checks not matching the issued-check file, but management must review exceptions promptly. The bank tie beats the GL for cash; never assume the ledger is correct.

Changes to vendor bank details deserve heightened control: independent callback using established contact information, change-log review, delayed activation where appropriate, and segregation between maintenance and payment release. Email instructions alone are weak evidence because business-email compromise can mimic a vendor.

IT-dependent and automated controls

An automated three-way match is reliable only if configuration, access, source data, and change management are controlled. General IT controls over user access, program changes, operations, backup, and interfaces support application controls. A spreadsheet reconciliation is an end-user computing tool and needs version control, protected formulas, input validation, review evidence, and retention.

Test design separately from operation. Inspect configuration to evaluate design; select transactions across the period to evaluate operation. Reperformance provides stronger evidence than inquiry alone. If a reviewer signs a reconciliation without investigating a variance, the sign-off does not prove the control's objective was achieved.

Journal-entry and access controls

Manual journal entries need a defined preparer, independent approver, business purpose, supporting schedule, exact accounts, entity, date, and post-entry validation. System-enforced balance is necessary but insufficient. Monitor entries posted by privileged users, outside normal hours, to unusual accounts, with round amounts, or near close. Reversing entries should link to the original and execute in the intended period.

User access reviews compare active accounts and privileges to current job duties. The reviewer needs a readable role-to-permission mapping; approving a list of usernames without knowing their access is not precise. Investigate dormant accounts, terminated users, shared IDs, excessive administrator rights, and incompatible combinations such as vendor maintenance plus payment release.

Changes to interface mappings and checkbook configuration require testing and approval before production. Retain old and new values, requester, developer/configurer, tester, approver, deployment time, and rollback plan. Emergency changes receive expedited authorization and prompt retrospective review; “emergency” cannot become the normal bypass.

Finally, retain evidence in a controlled location. Email approval without the attached report, query parameters, or exception resolution cannot prove what was reviewed. A reproducible control package includes source extracts, transformation logic, control totals, exceptions, and reviewer conclusions.

General, application, and transaction controls — the taxonomy

The blueprint distinguishes general accounting system controls from application and transaction controls, and the distinction decides what a test proves. General controls operate across applications: access provisioning, program change management, program development, computer operations, and physical security over the environment. Application controls operate inside one process and are usually classified by where they act in the processing cycle.

Input controls

  • Field check — the data type is right (an account field contains digits, not text).
  • Validity check — the value exists in a master file (the job number is an active MBG job).
  • Limit check — the value is below a ceiling (no single invoice line above $250,000).
  • Range check — the value falls between a floor and a ceiling (posting period 1 through 12).
  • Sign check — the value carries the expected sign (a WIP cost line is a debit).
  • Completeness check — every required field is populated (entity, job, cost code, approver).
  • Reasonableness test — the value is plausible against a related field (400 payroll hours for one employee in one week is not).
  • Check digit — a computed digit appended to an identifier detects transposition (vendor 40817 keyed as 48017 fails).
  • Batch control totals — record count, financial total, and hash total computed at the source and re-computed at the destination.

Processing and output controls

Processing controls include run-to-run totals carried between programs, sequence checks on serially numbered documents, matching routines such as the three-way match, and duplicate-transaction detection on a stable key. Output controls include distribution restriction, reconciliation of report totals to control totals, error-listing review, and retention of the exception report with evidence that each exception was cleared.

Worked example — batch control totals pinpoint the missing record

A record count and a dollar total are complementary, and a third control — the hash total — turns a detection into an identification. A hash total sums a field that has no business meaning as a sum, such as vendor identification numbers, purely so that a change in the population changes the sum.

An illustrative PayStream-to-JCS interface batch is prepared and re-computed at the destination:

Control totalSource (PayStream)Destination (JCS)Difference
Record count1201191 record
Financial total$486,320.15$485,570.15$750.00
Hash total of vendor IDs1,447,9081,433,90814,000

Work the three differences together. One record is missing. Its amount is $486,320.15 − $485,570.15 = $750.00. Its vendor identification number is 1,447,908 − 1,433,908 = 14,000. The reviewer now queries the source for vendor 14000 with a $750.00 line and retrieves the exact record, rather than eyeballing 120 rows. Had only the financial total been used, the reviewer would know $750.00 was missing but not from where; had only the record count been used, the reviewer would know one record was missing but not its size.

The correct response is to reload the identified record through the controlled interface with the same batch identifier, then re-run all three totals to $0.00 difference. The wrong response is to post a $750.00 plug to force the tie, which leaves the destination balanced, the population still incomplete, and the underlying interface defect unfixed and certain to recur.

Trap that loses the mark — believing a balanced destination is a complete one

Interfaces frequently drop matched debit and credit pairs together, because a rejected transaction is rejected in whole. The destination stays in balance while records vanish. This is exactly why the assertion tested by a control total is completeness, and why completeness is tested with counts and unique identifiers rather than with balance.

Worked example — quantifying segregation-of-duties conflicts

With four incompatible functions — authorization, custody, recordkeeping, and reconciliation — there are 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 possible incompatible pairs. A segregation matrix lists the pairs down one axis and users across the other, and the measurable output is a conflict rate.

An illustrative access review of the purchase-to-pay application covers 42 active users. Nine hold both vendor-master maintenance and payment release.

  • Conflict rate = 9 ÷ 42 = 21.43% of active users hold the highest-risk pair
  • The rate is meaningful only if the denominator is the complete active population — terminated users still provisioned, service accounts, and contractor logins all belong in it

Nine conflicted users is not automatically nine findings. For each, ask whether the access is used, whether a compensating control operates with sufficient precision, and whether the role is required by the size of the team. Compensating controls for this specific pair include independent review of all vendor-bank-detail changes against callback evidence, review of the positive-pay exception file by someone outside AP, a post-payment analytic comparing payee bank details to the approved vendor master, and monthly bank reconciliation performed by a person with no payment authority. A compensating control must address the same risk at the same level of precision — an annual review of a monthly risk does not compensate.

Function heldPaired withWhat the combination enables
Vendor master maintenancePayment releaseCreate a payee and pay it
Invoice entryInvoice approvalRecord and authorize a fictitious obligation
Cash custodyBank reconciliationTake the cash and hide the difference
Payroll master maintenanceTime approvalCreate a ghost employee and approve their hours
Journal entry preparationJournal entry approvalPost an unsupported adjustment to conceal any of the above

Trap that loses the mark — confusing recording with authorization

An accountant who prepares a journal entry is performing recordkeeping, not authorization, and there is nothing wrong with that. The conflict arises only when the same person also approves the entry, or holds custody of the asset it affects. Exam questions test whether you can classify a duty before you judge it. Classify first — authorization, custody, recording, reconciliation — then look for a person holding two.

CPA Crossover — AUD and ISC

AUD focuses on walkthroughs, control testing, and audit response. ISC focuses on access, interfaces, change management, system development, and data integrity. Both ask whether information used in a control is complete and accurate. An impressive dashboard is not evidence until its source and transformation are validated.

Practice and recap

  1. Draw the transaction flow across JCS, Ledgerline, PayStream/Apex, and the bank.
  2. Mark authorization, custody, recording, and review roles.
  3. Define interface counts and dollar control totals.
  4. Reconcile gross-to-net payroll, liabilities, payment, and job allocation.
  5. Validate checkbook-to-entity-to-GL mapping.
  6. Investigate exceptions; do not plug them.

Recap: segregation of duties makes concealment harder, while reconciliations connect independent evidence. Multi-system control succeeds only when every record retains its entity, account, job, period, and authorization from source to destination.

flashcards.front: What four functions should be segregated?
What are MBG's real primary systems?
flashcards.back: JCS job-cost GL; Ledgerline for MBG Multifamily; PayStream and Apex Staffing for payroll; First Regional Bank for primary banking.

flashcards.front: What does an interface reconciliation prove?
flashcards.back: Completeness, accuracy, cutoff, and validity from source to destination.

flashcards.front: Why use both record counts and dollar totals?
flashcards.back: Equal dollars can hide missing/duplicate records, while equal counts can hide amount errors.
An alternative control that addresses the same risk when ideal segregation is impractical.
The bank statement and reconciliation; the bank tie beats the GL.

flashcards.front: What labor payment methods follow MBG convention?
flashcards.back: PayStream ACH or MBG check; never cash labor.

flashcards.front: Why do automated controls depend on IT general controls?
flashcards.back: Access, changes, operations, and data integrity determine whether configured automation remains reliable.

quiz.title: Control Activities and Segregation of Duties

questions.q: Which combination creates the greatest segregation-of-duties risk?
choices: Create vendor, change bank details, enter invoice, and release payment
questions.explain: The same person can initiate, record, execute, and conceal an unauthorized payment.

questions.q: Illustrative gross pay is $50,000, employee withholding $10,000, net ACH $40,000, and employer tax $6,000. Total labor plus employer burden is:
questions.explain: $50,000 gross labor plus $6,000 employer burden equals $56,000; withholding is already part of gross pay.

questions.q: A source has 120 lines/$56,000 and destination 119 lines/$55,250. What should happen?
choices: Trace the missing $750 record and count difference
questions.explain: Counts and amounts indicate an interface exception requiring record-level investigation.

questions.q: Which system is the MBG job-cost GL?
questions.explain: JCS is the job-cost GL and must not be mislabeled Ledgerline 100.

questions.q: What is the strongest control over a vendor bank-detail change?
choices: Independent callback using established contact information plus segregated approval
Let the AP clerk change and pay
questions.explain: Independent verification and segregation reduce business-email-compromise and unauthorized-change risk.

questions.q: An automated match is reliable only when:
choices: Configuration, access, source data, and changes are controlled
questions.explain: Automation inherits risks from configuration, data, and IT general controls.

questions.q: Why is a reviewer signature insufficient by itself?
choices: It does not prove variances were investigated or the information was reliable
questions.explain: Operating effectiveness requires evidence of the review's precision and resolution, not a ceremonial sign-off.
